decks.primer:
Welcome to Sorcery's Druidic Order! You have been charged with the sacred duty of reclaiming the holy woodlands. Read on to arm yourself with the knowledge and tools needed to ensure victory!


Ever since the release of Arthurian Legends, I've been quite intrigued by [[Druid]]. In my opinion, this avatar has some of the deepest deck-building options and as such, you never know what you're up against when you see a Druid across the table. The flexibility of build options and three powerful abilities allows Druid to adapt to any metagame. This may or may not actually be a good thing from a game design perspective but it has been a very fun puzzle for me as a deckbuilder.


Sylvan Crusade was designed to attack a very specific expected meta for Season 6 of the TTS League. As this particular list evolves, I'll make notes in the "Card Choices" section to shed light on why certain cards are or are not included based on the current meta. Additionally, I’m going to preserve the original list for posterity.

If you're interested in checking out my other Druid decks, I've included a section at the very end of the primer with links and brief descriptions.


On the surface, Sylvan Crusade looks very similar to the classic Earth/Air Sorcerer Midrange decks of yesteryear and I'm honestly not certain that Druid is a more competitive choice over [[Sorcerer]] for this style of deck. The raw power of Sorcerer is undeniable at this point but, when you start to include a lot of spells that cost 5+ mana, the Sorcerer's ability to cast multiple spells each turn begins to diminish. Is a heavier top end at the expense of card quantity worth it? I think that a lot more testing is required to definitively answer that question but for now, I'm leaning towards yes! Yes, but...you need to leverage the abilities on Druid to make up for the card advantage of Sorcerer.

Historically, the Earth/Air package of beefy minions paired with [[Grapple Shot]] and [[Earthquake]] has been a very effective way to beat Fire-heavy Sorcerer aggro decks like Fury Road or Zalem's Fire/Air deck.

When I was looking at the decks used for qualifier rounds by players in the top cut for Season 6, Sorcerer aggro seemed to have a very hefty meta share. There were also a handful of other aggro decks with [[Flamecaller]], [[Avatar of Air]], and [[Battlemage]]. If players kept with whatever archetypes they used most during the qualifying rounds, there were going to be about 18-19 aggro decks (primarily Sorcerer/Fire), 8-9 [[Archimago]] decks (control or combo), and a small handful of other midrange or combo decks. This data led me to the conclusion that I wanted a deck that had an excellent matchup against Sorcerer aggro while not completely folding to Archimago control. I expected virtually no traditional midrange in this top cut as the general sentiment was that Archimago had pushed it out of the meta.

I considered just going with the old Earth/Air Sorcerer option in the hopes that the card draw would be enough to keep pace with Archimago's overwhelming amount of removal. After some deliberation though, I decided that I wanted to have fun with Druid even if it meant that I was going with a deck that might not be optimal. I still really liked the idea of out-muscling aggro with large Earth minions and I had also seen good results with Grapple Shot paired with [[Bruin]] in my Fire/Air aggro builds. I chose to lean into the aggressive end of the curve a little more to fight Archimago. I figured that most of the control versions were going to have the risk of stumbling on threshold early and the best plan was to try to Door them before they got the threshold to cast [[Divine Healing]]. While the plan of early Death's Door against Archimago is still a good one, some of the cards that I included to pursue this goal ended up being very poor choices.

If I'd had more time to test the deck before top cut submissions were due, I think I would have realized that [[Highland Falconer]] and [[Palliburie Bats]] were not good options for this deck. Despite the fact that they pair well with [[Torshammar Trinket]] and offer some resilience against Earthquake, the reality is that they don't line up well against [[Vile Imp]] and [[Quarrelsome Kobolds]] from the Fire aggro decks and they are particularly bad against all of the [[Magic Missiles]] and [[Firebolts]] from Archimago.

Overall, the deck performed very well though and with a few adjustments, I'm super happy with the current list.


Best cards for specific matchups:


Sorcerer aggro (fire) - [[Bosk Troll]], [[Autumn Unicorn]], [[Daperyll Vampire]], [[Sir Galahad]], [[Earthquake]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Crusade]], [[Ring of Morrigan]], [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Shield Maidens]], [[Root Spider]], [[Pillar of Zeiros]], [[Pebbled Paths]], [[Quagmire]], [[Pudge Butcher]]. If your Sorcerer opponent is on Air with Palliburrie Bats, Root Spider becomes much worse and if you're against a Water aggro deck, Earthquake is obviously pretty horrible.


Flamecaller aggro - Same list as above but include [[Funeral Pyre]].


Archimago control - [[Dwarven Digging Team]], [[Shield Maidens]], [[Pudge Butcher]], [[Grandmaster Wizard]], [[Gigantism]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Funeral Pyre]], [[Rift Valley]], [[Kingdom of Agartha]], [[Crusade]], [[Pnakotic Manuscript]].


Avatar of Air - [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Daperyll Vampire]], [[Sir Galahad]], [[Earthquake]], [[Crusade]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]], [[Rift Valley]], [[Ring of Morrigan]]


Mirror Match - [[Torshammar Trinket]], [[Pudge Butcher]], [[Dalcean Phalanx]], [[Root Spider]], [[Earthquake]], [[Grapple Shot]], [[Whirling Blades]].



Card Choices:


[[Bosk Troll]], [[Autumn Unicorn]] - These two minions have some of the most aggressive stat lines in the game and contribute to a critical number of beaters with high power to mana ratios. This is important both for stifling early aggression from aggro opponents and putting solid pressure on Archimago in the early game. Many of the best opening hands include one or both of these cards.


[[Pudge Butcher]], [[Dalcean Phalanx]] - While these minions come with serious mobility restrictions, 5 power for 4 mana is still a fantastic rate and when you pair them with mobility spells such as [[Blink]] or Grapple Shot they become incredibly dangerous. If you don't have mobility options, both of these cards can be a liability against aggro decks. If you are playing against aggro and your opening hand has one or more of these and you don't have Grapple Shot, Blink, or an early minion such as Bosk Troll or Autumn Unicorn, you'll probably want to mulligan them away. Summoning either of these on turn 3 using the extra mana from a Tower is one of the best early plays possible.


[[Root Spider]] - Still one of the best ways to shut down aggro and with Torshammar Trinket, it gets to win the fight against opposing spiders! If you're expecting a Water-heavy meta, or a significant amount of minion-light decks like Archimago or Battlemage, you can certainly trim some number of Root Spiders.


[[Daperyll Vampire]] - While this card has my least favorite art in the whole game, it is an incredibly powerful minion and puts in solid work against most opponents. The list that I used in Season 6 only had one copy of this card and that was a mistake. If you're expecting a lot of aggro in the meta, you should run the full 3 copies. This is one of the best things you can combo with Grapple Shot or [[Whirling Blades]] and it's also dreamy with Torshammar Trinket.


[[Grapple Shot]] - Grapple is still one of the most powerful cards in the game and this list wants the full 4 copies. It is fantastic with any large minion and is particularly sweet with [[Bruin]]. The only downside to Grapple is that you need a minion on the board for it to work and keeping a suitable minion alive can often be a challenge. Being able to flip Druid and immediately Grapple with Bruin is an awesome option.


[[Whirling Blades]] - While this card doesn't work optimally with Dalcean Phalanx and doesn't work at all with Pudge Butcher it is wildly powerful and goes well with just about every other minion in the deck.


[[Earthquake]] - My vote for best Earth card to date! This deck gets to leverage the movement of sites very well with Pudge and Phalanx.


[[Gigantism]] - Another of Earth's most powerful cards here. If you've got 7 mana, Gigantism and Grapple Shot, it's usually enough to Door your opponent in one turn.


[[Blink]] - The best mobility spell there is right now. Blink is necessary for most decks that include things like Pudge Butcher or Dalcean Phalanx and surprise movement is one of the most effective ways to win games.


[[Dwarven Digging Team]] - This card is one of several concessions to the prevalence of Archimago. In many games against Archimago control, your best route to victory is to chip your opponent down to around 15 life and then set up a big attack to Door them on a single turn, thus negating Divine Healing. Being able to build up a small army underground and then pop up for a huge attack is one of the best ways that I've found to accomplish this. Dwarven Digging Team also helps combat enemy Root Spiders. This card is not very good against aggro and I would mulligan it if I was up against Sorcerer, Flamecaller, Avatar of Air, or Battlemage.


[[Kettletop Leprechaun]] - This unassuming little fellow is actually very effective in this deck. Since this deck is interested in going up to 6+ mana - especially if it's a matchup where you want to keep [[Tawny]] around as long as possible - anything that draws a site during the early game is about as good as drawing a spell. Having 2 power makes in considerably better than [[Land Surveyor]] in a deck like this that is looking to get aggressive and even smaller minions can become real threats with Torshammar Trinket and [[Crusade]]. The 4 copies that I had in the original list felt like too many and 2 copies has been feeling pretty good.


[[Shield Maidens]] - Not including this card in my Season 6 list was a mistake. It is incredibly powerful against Fire-heavy aggro and provides your whole team with protection against [[Poison Nova]] from Archimago.


[[Sir Galahad]] - This card looked like it was going to be pretty solid but I was not prepared for just how incredible it actually is in the current meta. It prevents damage from some of the most popular minions such as Vile Imp, Pudge Butcher, Daperyll Vampire, and [[Headless Haunt]]. It is very difficult to kill in combat or with damage-based removal and it even survives [[Chaos Twister]] if it lands on a site (with split power/toughness, Chaos Twister adds both numbers together and divides by 2 before rounding up. This means that Galahad only deals 5 damage if it lands on a site after being targeted by Twister). You can also use Pudge Butcher to fight Galahad if you really need to gain 3 life.


[[Grandmaster Wizard]] - The Season 6 list had a single [[Unlikely Alliance]] as a way to catch back up on cards against Archimago. Alliance worked nicely with Highland Falconer/Palliburie Bats and Tawny/Bruin but with the Falconer/Bats package out of the deck, it just isn't reliable enough. Grandmaster Wizard is 6 mana but it is a guaranteed 3 spells which is exactly what this deck wants on later turns. With 3 copies of Trinket in the deck, the 0-power body isn't completely irrelevant either!


[[Highland Princess]] - Any deck that is running good 1-mana artifacts and can get 2 Air threshold should probably include Princess.


[[Disenchant]] - This is a card that is very meta-dependent and always comes with the risk of being a dead draw. I still think it's probably worth including a single copy but I also think you could easily trim it and be fine.


[[Torshammar Trinket]] - This card is so good with Tawny that I really like including the full 3 copies. It makes most combat situations favorable for you on your turn, can't be hit with removal like Disenchant, and is insane with Ring of Morrigan. I think that Trinket is one of the best cards in the current meta.


[[Ring of Morrigan]] - Ring good.


[[Philosopher's Stone]] - With a good mix of multiple elements, Philosopher's Stone is still among the most useful cards available.


[[Pnakotic Manuscript]] - This card is very good with Tawny but can also be used by Dalcean Phalanx or Pudge Butcher of their movement restrictions are preventing them from being effective. I'm still not 100% certain that this card belongs in this list but I do like it and we'll see how further testing goes.


[[Crusade]] - Once you get to around 20 Earth minions in your deck, Crusade starts looking very appealing. Archimago uses a lot of defensive sites like [[Perilous Bridge]] and [[Gnome Hollows]] and Crusade allows you to skip right over those cards. It's also one of the best ways to fight against [[Jihad]] from the Fire aggro decks. Keep in mind that Bruin is a Earth minion and will get the +1!


[[Feast for Crows]] - while this card is particularly bad against aggro, it is incredibly useful against Archimago. I think that this deck has a good enough matchup against aggro to afford a few cards like this and still be ok.


[[Dark Tower]]/[[Gothic Tower]]/[[Lone Tower]] - The best mana accelerant sites in the game. Jumping the curve on early minions is one of the best paths to victory.


[[Funeral Pyre]] - No Fire, 3 Pyre! Archimago is this much of a problem. Typically decks with threshold requirements like this can afford 3-5 off-element, utility sites. I would love to be able to play more [[Wizard's Den]], [[Sinkhole]], [[Free City]], [[Town]], etc., but stripping Archimago of cards is just too important right now. You'll also be happy to see Pyres against any [[Deathspeaker]] opponents you run across.


[[Glastonbury Tor]]/[[The Colour Out of Space]] - While both of these sites can be a liability against opposing Earthquakes they are a necessary inclusion for the threshold requirements. If you're playing against an Earth opponent, try to spread them out so they can't both be hit by the same Earthquake.


[[Impenetrable Copse]] - Copse is fantastic against Archimago and other decks using Grapple Shot or Pudge Butcher.


[[Kingdom of Agartha]] - There is some tension between this card and the two copies of Earthquake but Kingdom is so good against Archimago that I think it's worth the risk.


[[Mirror Realm]] - It's rare that a deck doesn't want Mirror Realm and this certainly isn't one of those rare decks.


[[Pebbled Paths]]/[[Quagmire]] - These are the two most effective Earth sites when you're facing against Fire aggro. With how much charge is in the meta right now, I think that pretty much all heavy-Earth decks want a good number of these sites.


[[Pillar of Zeiros]] - Deathspeaker has fallen off considerably in past months but the healing effect from Pillar is still very useful.


[[Rift Valley]] - One of the best sites in the game, Rift Valley should be included in just about every Earth deck.


[[Valley of Delight]]/[[Windmill]] - Great fixing for multi-element decks.


[[Watchtower]] - While [[Infiltrate]] isn't seeing as much play right now, it is still out there and one of the best things against your large minions. [[Morgana le Fay]] and [[Phase Assassin]] are also two big metagame players right now.


[[Wizard's Den]] - With very few options for drawing additional spells, Wizard's Den is a welcome inclusion and I wish that I could fit the second copy in here. If you expect less Archimago, you can definitely swap out a Funeral Pyre for an extra Den.


[[Highland Falconer]]/[[Palliburrie Bats]] (currently out of the deck) - This package works really well against decks that use things like [[Bury]] or Earthquake as their primary removal. They are also fantastic at driving out enemy Root Spiders. The two bodies that you get when you cast Falconer are nice with Torshammar Trinket. This package is currently out of the deck because Archimago has a ton of things like Magic Missiles and the Fire aggro decks have Vile Imp and Quarrelsome Kobolds.


[[Unlikely Alliance]] (currently out of the deck) - With the removal of Highland Falconer and Palliburrie Bats, this card just isn't reliable enough.


[[Vanguard Knights]] (currently out of the deck) - I really like that Vanguard Knights can be played off of a turn 1 Earth site into turn 2 Tower (something that Autumn Unicorn can't). It is also really cool that you can sneak the Knights onto Gnome Hollows. If you start their movement as 2-power they don't become 4-power until they're actually on the Hollows. This card can be incredibly awkward and ultimately, I've decided to bench it for now.


[[Atlas Wanderers]] (currently out of the deck) - While the ability on this card can be very useful, the triple Earth threshold and the fact that it isn't significantly more powerful than most of the other minions at the 4-5 mana range led me to cut the single copy that I had in my initial list.


[[Bury]] (currently out of the deck) - The Fire-based aggro decks have tons of small minions that make Bury feel underwhelming. Archimago has virtually no minions that you care about so Bury is just a weaker Disenchant for their artifacts. If non-water midrange makes more of a comeback, I would put Bury back in but for now, it's out and the cut has been feeling correct.


[[Common Sense]] (currently out of the deck) - With 0 copies of Bury, the Common Sense package began to look too small. The flexibility is nice for sure but so far, I haven't been missing it much in testing.



Notable Exclusions:


[[Dream-Quest]] - Even though this deck is looking to keep Tawny around for as long as possible, I don't like that Dream-Quest is mostly dead once you flip Druid. Additionally, the core of this deck is mostly just interchangeable, large minions and removal. Many Druid decks do want Dream-Quest but I don't think that this is one of them.


[[Drums of Doom]] - This deck is already very good at beating minion-heavy aggro decks and I didn't feel like I needed the help of Drums for those matchups. Since this is a deck with lots of large minions that are already going to dominate most combat situations, Drums can end up backfiring really badly for you (particularly against Fire) by allowing your opponents' smaller minions to trade up. Finally, Drums does virtually nothing against Archimago. With all of this in mind, it didn't make sense to include them.



Other Druid lists that I've been tuning:


Sylvan Crusade with a Dash of Fire - With Glastonbury Tor, The Colour out of Space, 3 Funeral Pyre, and Valley of Delight already in the deck, I figured that I could add in a few additional Fire sites and splash for [[Poison Nova]]. Nova is really good with Tawny and Shield Maidens and while I'm not sure that this splash is better than sticking to Earth/Air, it has been working well enough to warrant further testing.


Heavy Meta Druid - This list dips deeper into Fire for things like [[Morgana le Fay]], [[Sir Balin]], [[Sir Kay]], [[Sir Morien]], and [[Pact with the Devil]] while retaining a good amount of the beefy Earth package.


Swamp Song - This is the least tested of my Druid decks and I think also the weakest in the current meta. It uses lots of Water sites to play around Earthquake while tapping into a flexible menagerie of Beasts and Mortals.


The Art of War - A hyper-aggro Fire/Air deck that goes all in on charge minions and splashes for Grapple Shot. Lots of the proximity spells in Fire work nicely with [[Tawny]]!


Druid's Deep - My original Druid deck that is mostly Water with a splash of Air for things like [[Grapple Shot]] and [[Dream-Quest]]. This deck has lots of massive, top-end minions like [[Diluvian Kraken]] and [[Great Old One]].

decks.primer:
Introduction + Acknowledgments

This deck is based on the original and AL edits to Fury Road from @Sorcelled.


I've been intrigued by Fury Road ever since @abarth, a fellow Beast of the Bay, showed up to a meetup with a copy of it. I kept modifying some parts of it to better fit my play style (adding [[Sinkhole]]s, removing things like [[Gigantism]]) and played it at Quest for the Crown to a top 4 finish, losing only to the aforementioned @abarth, who won that event. I further refined my decklist to what I played in the Finals of Yeticon 2025 vs. @Sorcelled.


This is my take on the deck. It is definitely crafted to my playstyle, so there are choices that are unique to me (i.e. no more [[Sleeping Giantess]], no need for Deserts, etc.). I welcome comments and feedback.


Sin City Open 2025 Tournament Result

There were 17 players in the Sin City Open 2025 event that took place in Las Vegas, Nevada on Friday, January 17, 2025.


Round 1: Win 1:0 vs. Justin Watte with [[Archimago]] (Earth/Air)

This game went a bit over time because we got started late. Justin put together quite a lot of pressure with [[Border Patrol]], and eventually I was on Death's Door with him having prevented me from getting him to Death's Door with a [[Root Spider]] for my pair of [[Brother Knight]]s. I had cleared most of the board when he got out [[The Ninth Legion]]. They were just too slow to catch up to my [[Sorcerer]] running around the board though, and I was able to drop Justin to 0, and finish up with the killing blow.


Round 2: Win 1-0 vs. Brian Vegso with [[Deathspeaker]]

I almost lost this game essentially on turn 1. Brian started the game with a turn 2 [[Thunderstorm]] placed right atop my avatar. Rather than play a second site in front of my avatar (because it would also still be subject to the aura), I played my second site to the left. I summoned a [[War Horse]], which picked up my Sorcerer and brough them to safety on the new site. This got me away from the storm, and let me still continue to build resources. A few turns later I had enough charge minions to take Brian to Death's Door, and then win the game.


Round 3: Win 1-0 vs. Jared Miller

To be written


Round 4: Win 1-0 vs. Neil Troy with [[Druid]] (Earth/Air)

We had tested this matchup just before the event, and it very much went in Neil's favor. In this round, however, Neil didn't draw enough early pressure, and I was able to pin down Tawny + a [[Bosk Troll]] with a [[Root Spider]] early in the game. This let me build up my mana, and then switch to 2 cards/turn mode, at which point I could start making more 1-for-1 and 2-for-1 trades of my own cards for the remainder of Neil's minions. Neil had an early Angel's Egg, so instead of spending my charge minions early to just get in for ~1 damage, I saved them for getting rid of Neil's minions, and for future assaults. In discussing the game right afterwards, Neil and I settled on this being an example of properly assessing who's the beatdown. By establishing myself in a more control role, I was able to better utilize my cards to neutralize the few threats being presented. I eventually drew into a [[Morgana Le Fay]], which gave me a [[Ring of Morrigan]]! Morgana eventually helped with removing the [[Angel's Egg]], which allowed me to quickly drop Neil to 0.


Thoughts

[[War Horse]] remains one of the best cards in the deck, almost singlehandedly being responsible for my win in round 2. Charge minions are powerful (and [[Pebbled Paths]] are plentiful), so finding other interesting spots to leverage their speed is critical. I am less convinced of the powers of [[Redcap Powries]], hence already having cut them to 2. [[Sinkhole]] remains very effective for me, and there was definitely a point where I was able to destroy a site, fill it in with a new site of my own, and charge forward.


Prizes!

I won a sweet Superbowl-style ring with a Pathfinder on it that says "Sin City Open 2025 Sorcery Champion". I also selected an event-stamped [[The Colour Out of Space]] and got it signed by some of the other folks who were there. I wore the ring for the Old School event the next day as well.

decks.name: S5 league winner - Grapple Island (40-20)
decks.primer:
Intended for competitive play

*******************************************************************


Overall: This is a control combo deck. Leviathan + graple shot being your 'combo'. The core of the deck is control combo. Dont activate leviathan unless you can at least hit twice. Try to door with leviathan combo by sneaking 4 damage somewhere. Use lightbolt/graple/firebolt/kobolds as finishers.


Note: This is not an easy deck to play. Sometimes you draw the wrong half of your deck against a matchup and lose but site placement can help mitigate that quite a bit.


Matchup Info:

Deathspeaker - slight disadvantage, dont feed them free creatures. Save common sense for early summoning/jihads. play curse on you in the endgame to prevent jhin OTK for a turn or two before they have the mana. Use courtesan to waste their resources once they've started to draw a lot or door them with their own jhin! Non jhin lists are favored.

Sorcerer (Cute/Goblins) - unfavored. Their general gameplan ignores some of your defences. Mariners curse and kobolds are your mvps. It really comes down to if you can draw what you need.

Sorcerer (fury road) - slightly favored. Jihad and a good rift valley will easily tilt it in their favor

Sorcerer (Air/Earth) - slight favored. straightforward matchup

Seer(Yg combo) - playable if you tech for it... If you see seer, dig for common sense/puffer fish early and dont deploy leviathan until pop. If you don't it goes from bad to absolutely terrible.

Other(yg combo) - even / slight advantage. The weakened beatdown/control strategy is something you can easily get ahead of and they will feel safe even with an empty board. Easy to OTK.

Battlemage - Favored, frogs and wheenies stem life lost early. Common sense package destroys artifact based BM.

Avatar earth - Slightly Favored. Displacing your lands puts you on the backfoot early and easily makes up for them having dead removal. The fire variant is harder to deal with as your chumpers die efficiently.

Avatar of air (air only) - Slight disadvantage. The free movement allows their already aggressive deck to be slightly faster. Don't give them free sites to attack or place harmful artifiacts. Muligan aggressively for eggs.

Sorcerer (spirits) - Strong disadvantage/slight disadvantage. Charge and stealth is a problem. If they are running haunts the matchup is even because that deck is a lot worse than big midrange spirits.

Deathspeaker(spirits) - Favored. Clumsy early aggro is easy to chump/deal with and you door them before their top end occurs. Don't feed them free creatures.

Sorcerer/PF(spell control) - Even. Lack of healing means all their spells are good when cast on you unless you draw your eggs. Threats are stick or do something as they come down so its usually always ok to let them die to removal.

Flamespeaker - Even. Can easily lose to great starts (jihad mainly) especially if you don't place your sites correctly

Big water decks - Slight disadvantage. You draw more cards and have decent cards against them. Can't deal with submerge so play around that and it's not bad. Use mariners curse to delay their attacks until they start stockpiling submerge minions. Really its who draws better. You win sideboard hard.

Enchantress (control) - advantage, you have more card advantage and the removal they run generally is reactive while also being threat light. Easy to OTK

Enchantress (aggro/midrange) - slight disadvantage / disadvantage depending on flavor. Some of your removal is hard to use on their threats and often gum up the board.


Mulligans:

-Mulligan lands aggressively for leviathan or threshold if you happen to draw princess in your opener.

-Generally mulligan sites until you hit island leviathan/tadpole pool for placement at site (2).

-Mulligan aggressively for the matchup in the spell card slots but keep obviously (slow) powerful cards if you feel comfortable with the sites you have.

-I generally snap keep princess, curse, land surveyor, and egg


Site placement:

Generally in order of placement

**3 2 3**

4 3 1 3 4


Minor note: Don't play non water sites at 2 or 3 if you are playing something you suspect has rift valley.


1 = dual land / leviathan

2 = bottomless pit / tadpole pool / geistwood ideally / leviathan / any water site

3 = anything, ideally leviathan

4 = non water sites because its easy to protect


General tips:

-You dont win early

-Try to stall your opponent with land placement and chump blockers with the defensive site placement stated above.

- leviathans + graple or a big ruler of thule turn

-try not to activate your leviathans right away unless you can door or the coast is clear (opponent is hellbent or is unlikely to have a good answer)

-Beware of rift valley on a non water site placed forward. Rift valley is the best anything against you.


Specific Tips:

-turtles + manuscript is a draw every turn without it dying.

-Quarrelsome kobolds can safely be placed on the backrow to setup ruler of thule/polar explorer turn

-Kobolds can be used to kill your minions on geistwood if you dont need to block if you opt to run it.

-if you arent feeling extreme pressure and have angels egg + frogs, submerge them so you dont get them disenchanted

-atlantean fate can clutch out your 8 water pips when you draw a lot of non water sites or make it safe to run out leviathans into bury.

decks.name: GenCon_2024 - 8th Place Constructed
decks.primer:
Kythera Mechanism: The ability to control my Haunt’s location and keep my opponent’s Haunts stuck in the void or dying in a Bottomless Pit in the mirror match was too good of an idea to pass up. If it ever mattered, I'd be able to determine my opponent’s lightning bolts if I had to choose between one of my minions and my AoA.


No Lightning Bolts for me? Yea... I was conflicted about that. Looking back, bye-bye Land Deeds, hello Lightning Bolts!


Sling Pixies: The MVP. Airborne + Ranged is a nasty combo. No wonder the design team only granted the Pixies with 1 power. As a fan of beefy minions, I never understood the significance of those little, early game pings until I played AoA. The goal is to create enough of a disparity in life total that your opponent feels like they're on their back foot by Turn 4 or 5; and while they continue to try and stabilize, you're still dropping minions, or Devil's Eggs and Madd. Bells to make their life even more miserable. Pixies can just hang out and ping the enemy with an undefendable strike every turn; it's Airborne makes it invulnerable to ground minions (without the help of additional spells); and with 3 Trinkets in the deck, it has the potential to deal up to 4 damage in one Ranged strike.

Against Roots, Pixies are FANTASTIC blockers against the opponent’s Amazon Warriors post-Root detonation. Post-Roots, the opponent's got 5-mana and casts Warriors. On our turn, we’ve got 1-mana, drop Pixies and block for days until we stabilize.




Splashing for Fire:

Smokestacks was already in the Atlas to turn off Roots or a Cloud City in the mirror match. My question became, how much more fire affinity can I add to the Atlas without detracting from my Air affinity while also providing enough Fire sites to run single-fire-threshold spells? The deck was already running Lighthouse, so swap those out for Ruins; that's 4 fire resources. Colour out of Space seemed so obvious for multiple reasons: 1. It provides Air and Fire, 2. It offers the same defensive capability as the Lighthouses (water sites) to ward off Root Spider, 3. AoA decks cap at 4 or 5 sites, so the chances of keeping Colour next to a void is pretty high; and in the extreme case I draw Colour and Smokestacks, Smokey just turns off Colour's limiting factor. Oh, and AoA can still treat it as an Air site to push things.

But what to remove? Every other site seemed so integral. As big of a fan boy as I am for Free City, one of the 3 copies had to go. Yes, they offer insane protection and can force your opponent to stall out while trying to figure out how to storm the castle. BUT, in a mirror match, Free City is lackluster being unable to attack enemy Airborne minions, AND it doesn't offer elemental affinity, so one copy had to go.


What fire spells are worth making the cut?

THIS was a tough question, but the end result (for better or worse) was a pair of Scarabs and a pair of Kobolds.


Sacred Scarabs: In my experience, fetching Scarabs with a Falconer feels like a total win until your opponent 2-for-1's you and removes both minions (it's happened more times than I care to admit). But in those situations, I wasn't piloting AoA. Simplest explanation: make sure AoA is on an Air site > cast Falconer on same site as AoA > fetch Scarab > use AoA to fly Scarabs to a nearby site where they won't grenade the home team for 3. Then your opponent has a much more difficult decision to make. If they stay on board until your next turn, ideally strap them with a Trinket or two, swing in, explode, and deal a total of 5 or 6 damage with Trinket(s) returning to your hand.


Quarrelsome Kobolds: Aggression. Aggression. Aggression. Cast them and push them as close to enemy unit as possible with AoA, then end the turn with a free, undefendable strike for 2 damage. Or is it 3 damage? Or 4, or 5? Because we're crazy enough to run 3 Trinkets. AoA loves its Gyre Hippos. Those Charging winged beasts feel so good to drop on turn 3 after a Dark Tower (my personal favorite Tower). From my pov, Kobolds are a 3-mana, 2-power minion with faux-Charge. If your opponent has played their sites aggressively enough to meet you in the middle of the board, ideally you've flown AoA to your forward most site on a previous turn > cast Kobolds on the same site as AoA > fly them straight ahead to bonk the enemy Avatar EOT who is probably still hanging out on their initial square.


Fire's Honorable Mentions: Blaze, Petrosian Cavalry, Pit Vipers, Wils-o-the-Wisp, Clamor of Harpies, Firebolts, Infiltrate and Poison Nova.


What did I learn after going 4-0 and then losing in the 5th and 6th round?

  • Land Deed wasn't worth it. I didn't get enough playtesting in to determine if I really wanted a pair of Land Deeds in there. However, in playtesting, I managed to get Madd Bells out by Turn 3 on the wings of a Bat and it caused such massive setbacks for my opponent it made me ask, "how can I make THAT more consistent?" Land Deed was the answer. In hindsight, I wish I could go back in time, slap me on the wrist and say "NO. Either you put the Bolts back in there or the Flanking Maneuver, but you are taking those Deeds out. Hell, put in a 4th Grapple Shot!"
  • In order to learn from my losses, it helps to remember the sequences that led to the loss. My Round 5 match against Zalem was brutal. By T3 he’d played (in this order): Free City, G Hollows, and Mirror Realm to copy Free City. The game was basically over; G Hollows locks out nearly 50% of my minions (Haunt, Phase Ass, Gyre Hippo and Dap Vamp); and Free City prevents me from attacking with 80% of my minions! For better or worse, I’m wired to never give up, so the game continued. I tried my best to attack his Hollows with my Bats and his Free Cities with my Haunts, until he dropped 2 Root Spiders by T4 and T5 under is Hollows. My only options at that point were to draw into a Smokestacks to shut down his FC and GH or put a Sling Pixies on his Free City and ping his Seer for 2 with Trinket. He Infiltrated my Bat on his third Hollow (the only one without a burrowed Root Spider) and used it to kill my Cloud Spirit attempting to enter the Hollows and join the meager assault. The most disheartening series of turns was when he cast a Scarecrow into the hands of Root Spider which prevented my burrowed Bat from entering and killing the Spider. The next turn he dropped 1 Angel’s Egg to the spider, and the turn after, a 2nd Angel’s Egg. In a matter of turns he'd completely inverted the life total. The entire game I never saw my Devil’s Eggs, Madd Bells or Boulders. All would’ve helped in their own way.
  • AoA benefits from splashing an element. Is Fire the best element to splash? I've been asking that since playtesting for GenCon. How I'd love to run Windmills for Earth, push my opponent's minions onto Air sites above my burrowed Root Spider, or Common Sense for a Grapple Shot or Bolt. Put the Lighthouses back in for Water and use Shrink help my small minions take out larger threats. But that's just one element (no pun intended) of the beauty of this game. There are so many options for creative answers. If I could go back, I would've put in 2 Pit Vipers, maybe 3, to handle enemy Root Spiders.
  • My Round 6 loss against Chris (I forget his last name) was pretty straightforward. He piloted AoE and ran me over with Earthquake and big minions. What can you say? Earth is good. Again, Pit Vipers would've been ideal, surviving Earthquake, and easily trading with any minion he put down. I don't recall drawing into my FC or BP which would've kept those ground minions at bay. Ultimately, I think I played my hand and the game in front of me the best I could. As the saying goes, you win some, you lose some.
  • Cheers!

decks.name: Midwinter Championship SECOND PLACE - Jarrod Scriven
BIRDS BIRDS BIRDS (1st Place League S4)
decks.primer:
Intro 🌟

Hi everyone, I'm Kevin. This is the list that I created over the course of the 4th Discord league, eventually taking the win with in the top cut. Potato Knight also ran the list, coming 3rd/4th, so effectively it went 7-0, losing only to itself.


The list is basically aggro fliers with artifact support. You slap down as many bodies as you can, split them up to avoid Poison Novas and Earthquakes, then use your aerial advantage to strategically pick your opponent apart while presenting a solid defence with free cities and bottomless pits.


Lots of the cards here are already covered by other AoA lists, so I'll stick to explaining my modifications.


Card Explanations 📄

[[Plumed Pegasus]] / [[Haast Eagle]]

The namesake of the deck, our birds (Eagles are just Pegasus with worse threshold). It took me the longest time to figure these out (thanks Duo!) but really glad I tested them. Flying [[Bosk Trolls]] might not sound impressive at first, but I believe airborne is a massively underrated ability. In Sorcery, minions are removal. Airborne removes the ability for our opponent to attack back, creating a unilateral beatdown - we can still use our minions as removal, while theirs are stuck defending. Combine this with Trinkets and you end up with an extremely annoying suite of minions (can't be easily imp'd, kolbods'd, or attacked) that usually at best is 1-for-1'd by our opponent. The best part is, we don't really care! Their low cost and our minion density means we're usually deploying a new one every turn - embracing this 'throw minions at your opponents face until they door' is the core philosophy of this deck.


Devil's Eggs

These bad boys let you win games that I otherwise consider unwinnable, or extremely grindy at best. You have many ways to get this to an annoying place (bats, cloud spirits, AoA herself), and once it sticks, it creates an immense amount of pressure for your opponent - the clock is ticking. Also cancels out Angel's Eggs, which more decks are running now to our chagrin (if you ever find a way to steal them, make sure you do!).


Maddening Bells

Bells are often seen in control/tax decks, but I think it's one of the most powerful aggro cards. Combined with your mobility and towers, you can fairly frequently land a bells on your opponent by turn 3. On the play, I've had opponents concede immediately. While one of the worst cards you can draw late game, it has led to so many blow outs I still keep it, if for nothing else but the mind games.


Cloud Spirit

A really solid 2 power minion. Sadly rarely get to play it on curve due the threshold, but a card that's as good late game as it is early - a universal blocker/attacker is a massive headache for your opponents to play around.


Headless Haunt

I was on the fence for the longest time with these (what if they fall into the Bottomless Pits!?) but now I'm a believer. Lots of people think that the randomness is a downside - it really isn't, it's more of a weird form of evasion - and that 3 cost 4 body is amazing. Play this deep in the void and watch your opponent sweat figuring out how to block it.


Sinkhole

After I tried bells, I had the realization that this is exactly what the deck needed - a way to keep the game in 'early game' for as long as possible. Sinkholes not only acts as an amazing utility card (blow up the roots combo, get rid of their threshold etc.), but is most importantly free mana denial. While you vomit fliers onto the board, your opponents are stuck with an earthquake and 3 mana. One of the best cards in the game, never remove this.


Cut Cards ✂️

Skirmishers of Mu

One of the more controversial cuts, but after testing a bunch I've decided it's for the best. While the synergy with AoA is undeniable, for a 4 cost investment (your whole turn in this deck), Skirmishers are too easy to play around and remove for opponents that know what's coming. It's one of those cards that feel great when you get to trinket it, swing for 8, but then you forget all the times it dies to a lightning bolt, or a firebolts, or swings for 3 then dies to a unicorn, etc.


Phantasmal Shades

Just barely cut, could be in sideboard. 3 cost 4 power is amazing, but it's ability requires too much baby-sitting for our liking. One theme you will notice with our minions is that they're all very 'independent'. We spread them out like little missiles and then forget about them. This causes all sorts of headaches for our opponent and allows our Avatar to boulder, swing herself, defend the sites, etc.


Daperyll Vampires

Extremely powerful against mirror match, and aggro in general. Sadly too expensive, slow, and vulnerable for our deck (read above). A great sideboard card though, I'll have a minimum of 2 of these there.


Hounds of Ondaros

I really like these guys - they're a massive PITA to remove, so don't fall under the same umbrella as Mu/Vamps/Shades - they're about as resilient/independent as it gets. Unfortunately, they also do nothing for the first 5 turns of the game, and their upside is an evasive bird with +1 power for +2 cost...so they're a cut.


Spectral Stalker

Cute turn 1 tower play aside, these don't do much but die to imps/kobolds.


Browse

Another controversial cut - this is probably the best late game top-deck in the game. Unfortunately, there will be many games where this sits dead in your hand for the first 5 turns - we often have trouble hitting 3 x Air due to the neutral sites, and 1 mana is also non-trivial due to our super low curve.


Chain Lightning

Arguably the best finisher in the game - with AoA it's basically an guaranteed kill. Unfortunately outside of that one specific use-case, I found the card to be quite underwhelming - while it can be used for 4 mana to kill 2 small minions, you usually have much better uses of 4 mana. The 2 mana mode is terrible (bolts is much better), and you'll basically never do it with 6+.


Thunderstorm

Very matchup dependant card; I just found it too clunky to use. Haven't tested with this enough though, PK insists it's the best card since Poison Nova. 4 mana is just a lot, and our list is already very tight.


Credits 🎉

Potato Knight for all the help with playtesting, repping the deck, and being awesome in general!

Wulfinite, DarthNunu, MattdogNZ, and CJ for being top blokes and encouraging me through the league!

Duo for our chat that inspired my initial testing of Plumed Pegasus!

Jacksun and Drew from OnThePlay for the initial inspiration behind playing the deck!

All the cool peeps I met playing the game on discord - you know who you are!

My amazing gf for playtesting and moral support, and pulling my foil AoA 😁


Finally, shout out to all the people that helped run the league, it was my first foray into competitive Sorcery and you guys made it super fun. Cheers!

decks.name: ANZ Championship Top 8 Elementalist
decks.primer:
My Elementalist control deck that managed to squeak into the top 8 at Plenty of Games in Melbourne 6/7 April. Good against minion-based aggro, Ok against other control builds, very poor against Avatar of Earth.

My biggest takeaway of the weekend is that I just wish I had more time to play and practise beforehand.The top 8 game was my second match against Enchantress ever, and it was definitely a trial by fire. I learned a lot, but made some poor decisions and misplays along the way, but as long as I can get people talking about the game, then that’s a big win in my book.

The build is something I’ve tinkered with over the last couple of months in league play, and it features some of my favourite cards that may not necessarily be tournament all-stars, but I enjoy them immensely.

It was a fantastic event, so big thanks to Jesse and the team at Plenty of Games.


Edit: The deck isn’t primarily a Roots deck, but has it as a backup plan to help regain board control. As such, it doesn’t recover super well compared to other builds. Instead the deck is more ramp and control to set up the Orb combo kill. As such the deck struggles against mobile avatars that are coming into your side of the board. I was hoping to play more sorcerer, where cards like poison nova help take away their card advantage. Geistwood is the most powerful card in the deck, and is probably a better mulligan than Roots a lot of the time.

decks.name: Community Day 1 - 1st Place - Kass Pathfinder Aggro
Tournament List + Primer
decks.primer:
Yo, so this list has been incredibly good in terms of results going a total of 43(61 as of 2024/01/09) wins, 7(19) losses and 1 draw(?) where we were both on deaths door and both died to a craterize. (Several hundrwd more games have been played, please refer to the bottom of this primer)


The deck's worst match up by far is avatar of earth which just aggro's you out of the game and kills you quicker than you can resource lock them, with an avatar that is big enough to fight over your bodies.

The deck has only a single loss(3 now) into death speaker so far, it becomes very easy to lock their resources before they have the djinn combo kill, and sometimes you can just avoid it entirely by sitting on a gnome hollows and deleting all the surrounding sites with lord of the voids.


basic sideboard plan:

enchantress

+3 disenchant

+2 root Spider

+1 Gnome Hollows

+1 Blink

+1 Nightmare


Battlemage

+2 Root Spider

+2 Daperyll Vampire

+1 Gnome Hollows

+1 Disenchant


Deathspeaker

+1 Nightmare

+1 Gnome Hollows

+1 Blink


Avatar of Earth

+1 Nightmare

+2 Rootspider

+1 Blink

+1 Gnome Hollows


Seer (this match up is wierd, i'v seen this deck built like 6 different ways)

+2 Daperyll Vampire

+2 Disenchant


Avatar of Fire

+1 Blink

+2 Root Spider


Elementalist

+1 Gnome Hollows

+2 Disenchant

+1 Nightmare


Pathfinder Mirror

+1 Blink

+2 Daperyll Vampire

+1 Nightmare


Avatar of Air

+1 blink

+1 Gnome Hollows

+2 Daperyll Vampire


Sorcerer

+2 Daperyll Vampire

+1 Nightmare

+1 Disenchant



As a general rule,. Vampire is in vs decks you suspect or know don't run scarabs. Blink is in vs matchups where they are happy to draw lands to block you or in matchups where they have few burn spells and blink offers ways to run from direct damage sources. Gnome Hollows is in vs avatars with greater than 3 power and against decks that look to combo kill you with a minion with 3 or more power. Disenchant is in vs decks that utilize artifacts or enchantments to gain an advantage. currently, this is only 2(usually) decks battle mage and enchantress, but the card is such a good tempo piece against enemy cores I like to bring it into decks that run 3+ colors as well because you can bet your ass they are running at least 3 cores and a p stone. Root Spider is in vs aggro, the card stalls the middle of the board stupidly well and effectively becomes a pillar you can kite around with your avatar. Nightmare is a tech piece and is overall an insanely underrated card that I believe is underutilized. It's a killspell, a huge body, and a utility piece all in one that you can usually play around turn 4 or 5. I play this card in matchups where I'm cutting 1 or more of the other larger bodies for color consistency, or into a match-up where I think the game will go long and I will need more threats to fight over the board state.


I hope this helps you to win some games, I know Pathfinder has been an absolute blast for me, and hope it can be for you as well.


One last idea I have been toying with is replacing the 2 frontier settlers with a second mix aer and a nightmare in the maindeck. many of our most unfair plays involve air cards so a second mix could be a way to decide games super early. playing a lord of the void, a nightmare or a masterwizard 3 or 4 turns ahead of schedule is pretty disgusting. It also free's up your early game threshhold requirements which is far and away the biggest issue this deck faces. The longer I type the more I'm convincing myself this is a change that should be tested further.


Update as of jan 11th:


The mix aer addition is great. Going up to 2 is fantastic. It replaced the monolith fully and lets you get off your late game plays early without the massive life commitment that would often times kill you into hyper aggro matchups. As it turns out - not vile imping your avatar every turn helps the aggro match up. Who would have thought.


Update - Jan 30th 2024:


I have now played close to 500 games with this deck and am happy with its current form. I'm sitting at 316 wins, 182 losses and a single draw giving me a 57.2% win/loss ratio. Over this many games i think i'm happy with that. I do not count my games playing against "non-optimized" decks. These are decks in which there are obvious upgrades that could improve them, but are omited for one reason or another -- usually price or scarcity. This deck has a nasty tendency to "pub-stomp" in the sense that it very quickly locks down the board if not quickly interupted with a timely dispel or bury for example. And recongnizing that this deck will overwhelm you if not interacted with early, is something that experienced players will realize, while newer players will take game after game to eventually pick up on. For this reason i also did not include games against newer players in my win to loss ratio. I wanted those numbers to be as realistic to a tournament setting as possible to provide the realest access to testing, and after many many games this is the final build i am happy with. I am now patiently waiting for aurthurian legends and all the potential new goodies it may promise.


I will update this primer, as well as the sideboard guide and decklist once the set drops and i playtesta bunch of games with the new cards!

decks.name: 2024 Tournament List - Heavy Aggro
decks.primer:
2024 LOCAL TOURNAMENT ENTRY LIST


BIG BODIES. BIG MANA. BIG WINS.


Update Feb. 10, 2024:

This is a lengthy walk through of the deck's updates and strategy, but give it a read if you're interested in how I find value in Sorcery card selection, and what an ideal play through for this deck looks like.


Deck has changed a bit after extensive play testing. I love the build and feel that it strikes the ideal balance of power and control. The number one goal is to put pressure on the opponent every turn. Below are a few updates with explanations about card choice:

  • Turn 0: You want to keep a hand that you know you can play, so mulligan anything over 4 mana to get started. There is enough card draw to find the big bombs again.
  • Turn 1: You're using Seer to filter into cards on curve, and to luckily dig up a Core or Phil Stone.
  • NOTE: You do NOT need to run expensive cards in this deck. The Stone and Cores can be swapped for Alvalinne Dryads and achieve the same effect. No one wastes a removal spell on Dryads that sit on your back row the entire game when you're dropping threats every turn anyway. The same goes for sites like Mirror Realm or Pillar - just swap them for sites of your choosing that you have, as they aren't part of any critical synergies like they would be in other decks.
  • Turn 2-3: Play Root Spider burrowed, Apprentice Wizard, or Autumn Unicorn as regularly as possible to apply pressure. Autumn Unicorn is tough to handle early when played on Turn 2. Vril Revenant was added as it became an awesome late game sink for mana. You've got nothing to lose by leaving it in the void where it can't even be targeted and saving it for an 8- or 9-damage strike later in the game. This card doesn't get enough play in my opinion.
  • Turn 4: You've hopefully played at least one card that lets you draw a spell, so draw a site and stay on curve by playing it. Look to cast a Chaos Twister or other spot removal spell to clear the way for any attacks you can make on enemy sites. Alternatively, if you're at 5 mana due to ramping with a core, playing Queen of Midland on your back row is huge. If you only get 2 cards out of her, that's on rate for Sorcery; whether you draw spells or sites, just make sure that you're playing a site each turn.
  • Turn 5: This is a pivotal turn for this deck. Turn 5 can be a bit uneventful for a slower deck or a deck that isn't geared toward maximizing pressure. You want to keep laying on the hurt. I gravitated away from some of the tougher minion choices in favor of cards that let us command value, like grandmaster Wizard. Playing him at this point is HUGE. either we're playing 2 smaller minions on this turn or we're playing something like GW that fills our hand. Remember to always make sure you're drawing and playing a site each turn instead of all spells.
  • Turn 6-7: This is where you try and put the opponent away. Playing Conqueror Worm, Wraetannis Titan, Undertaker Engine, or Earthquake puts your opponent on their heels. By now you've been able to play a total power of around 12-14 and should be able to clear the way next turn for a Death's Door attack.
  • Turn 8: By now one of two things have happened; 1) you've overwhelmed the opponent and played a solid threat every turn, allowing the minions to be the removal or 2) You've been trading blows with the opponent and have lost most minions the next turn due to removal. If a deck is more control-oriented and packs 20 Magic spells that all kill minions, then you can't do much to stop that. But what you can do is load up on the card draw spells in this deck and out-advantage your opponent in these crucial late game turns. If you have a thin board presence, then you've probably been playing minions over card draw spells up until this point only to watch them get removed quickly. Unload your card draw (there are 13 in the deck!), restock, and reclaim the board state. You're a three-legged stool; efficient minions, 11 removal spells, and 13 card draw spells to churn through the deck. I didn't take up lots of room in the card list for combo pieces and spells that do not directly contribute to this strategy. There are no "just in case" cards like Blasted Oak or Mordric Druids, etc.


I'll keep everyone posted as games progress, but this has become one of my favorite builds. It's a solid midrange deck that tries to hang tough no matter what the opponent does.



Update Jan. 4, 2024:

  • Have swapped in [[Seer]] for [[Pathfinder]].
  • Played more games Jan 3, and ran into too many players that know how to sandbag the Pathfinder. Playing your sites 1) beneath avatar, 2) in front of, 3) to side, 4) to side, 5) behind, 6) to side (essentially making a rectangle of 6 sites) is the most efficient layout to hit 6 mana on schedule. The problem is that the opponent is free to match our first 4 site plays, and then proceed from the other side towards our back end of the board while Pathfinder works its way along our bottom. You will only be able to drop 6 sites against an experienced player, which really hurts your ability to run a ramp strategy. [[Blink]] doesn't necessarily help, because you need to continue on a continuous path. I've swapped the[[Seer]] in at this time as the deck filtering is helpful in pulling the right spells to execute our steady ramp strategy. We have 12 spells that draw us a card (usually a spell) which can be used to offset our need to keep pumping out sites.


Update Dec. 28, 2023:

  • Trimmed down some one-of minions for more early and mid-game minions like [[Autumn Unicorn]].
  • Added more removal Magic like [[Infiltrate]] and [[Disintegrate]].
  • Considering removing [[Abundance]] due to its so-so performance. When it works it REALLY works, but otherwise you’re left wanting cards to play with all that mana.


Update Dec. 27, 2023:

  • Have swapped in [[Pathfinder]] for [[Elementalist]] and adjusted the Atlas to have one copy of each chosen site. Aiming to jam a few games in the next day or two to iron out the list, but it is pretty solid under these conditions.
  • Some newer players thought that Elementalist gave them extra mana; A reminder that it is only a threshold ability, and doesn't grant extra mana. If it were a philosopher's stone on a stick then it would be the most ubiquitous avatar in the game(!).



WELCOME:


(This is an out-of-date description, but I'm leaving it for the sake of record keeping)


This deck ramps into a highly aggressive list of minions that require nothing short of a board wipe in order to recover from. Early and frequent ramp along with card draw engines enable the casting of one or two huge bodies every turn. This is a ground-and-pound deck inspired by old school formulas, and is perfectly at home in the early Sorcery meta and card pool.


How does this deck work?

  1. Play your ramp spells like [[Alvalinne Dryads]] or [[Frontier Settlers]]. Your Relics like [[Philosopher's Stone]] and the cores help put you very ahead on mana which a lot of decks don't have much of an answer for.
  2. Play your threats as aggressively as possible, moving in to strike any opposing site or minion. You rely on a constant stream of heavy hitters, so keep casting and moving forward.
  3. Win conditions are achieved by sweeping the board with heavy attackers and cornering the enemy avatar, or by getting them to death's door in only a few turns' worth of attacks followed by a conveniently timed direct damage spell [[Craterize]], [[Lightning Bolt]] and [[Heat Ray]] are favorites.
  4. the deck is not going to win in only aha drum of turns. Sorcery is too balanced right now for anything degenerate. But the deck does have a momentum to it unlike anything else out there :)



A Tale of Three Avatars:

The deck was designed around [[Elementalist]] initially, but has switched to [[Pathfinder]] and [[Seer]] more recently to aid in guaranteed mana ramp and site drops.


Why use Seer?

  • [[Seer]] allows us to filter each turn for the right answer to an opponent, or to fish up the more ramp-oriented spells we rely on. Pathfinder proved to be tough to rely on when playing against an experienced player that would like to cut it off, and especially against an experienced player GOING FIRST.


Why use Pathfinder?

  • [[Pathfinder]] simply allows us to hit a site drop every turn while likely also drawing one of many ramp spells each and every turn. You don't want to miss a site play, and you also want to move around the board accordingly.


Why use Elementalist?

  • This avatar allows us to play a higher concentration of non-threshold Elite and Unique utility sites to gain extra board advantage. The Elementalist's threshold ability allows us to cast a lot of our spells without worrying about a threshold deficiency.
  • The [[Pathfinder]] avatar is another possible choice for this list. It ensures we can draw a spell every turn and never miss a site play, but the current avatar ended up proving to provide a tiny extra advantage with regard to the use of non-elemental sites for their added utility. The extra threshold and the ability to play more non-threshold sites is a really nice benefit. It is possible to swap in [[Pathfinder]] but you'd need to totally rethink the site list, which isn't a huge challenge.


What's next?

  • This deck is a list prepared for a small local event in 2024. I'll post updates and post-event results.


Thanks as always for any input, Sorcerers.

decks.name: 2024 Tournament List - Aggro Burrowing & Board Wipe
decks.primer:
2024 LOCAL TOURNAMENT ENTRY BUILD (EAST COAST, USA)


(For my other tournament entry build, see here: https://curiosa.io/decks/clqlpfv9i00i791u5rwyxvtq7)


"DIG 'N BURN"


UPDATE (1/24/2023)

Played some good water decks and a fairly competitive Pathfinder build and won both. Root Spider and Flame Wave are at the core of the long game when not playing against water, for sure. Sand Wurm proves vital in dealing chunk damage. By the late game it's tough to decide between Infernal Legion and playing a board-wide damage spell. By turn 6 you should have your opponent near death's door anyway.


When playing water you need to be defensive and lire the opponent onto your sites to cast removal like Cave-In or Bury. Burn spells help to some degree aside from that. A highly competitive water build does worry me a bit.

  • OUT: Salamander --> IN: Petrosian Cavalry
  • OUT: Dwarves --> IN: Pit Vipers

I'll post more updates. The deck needed more reliable ways to get early or mid-game minions out to start doing damage. Otherwise it is a fun build and can really hold its own.


What does this deck do?

Most importantly, this deck is super fun and makes you feel like you're forcing your opponent to play a nightmarish game of Whack-a-Mole. You'll see what I mean...Also, the deck creates synergies between its burn and board wipe spells, and its burrowing or fire-immune minions:


A typical play pattern goes as follows:

  1. On turns 1 thru 3 play [[Pit Vipers]], [[Dwarven Digging Team]] or [[Root Spider]] burrowed.
  2. Advance your burrowed minions while leading up to a burrowed [[Sand Worm]].
  3. Cast removal spells like [[Earthquake]] or [[Cave-In]] while all of your minions are safe underground.
  4. Curve into [[Askelon Phoenix]] on turn 5. You can ideally cast [[Flame Wave]] as soon as possible to wipe the board and have all of your burrowed minions survive. Phoenix will get buffed and swing in for big damage along with all of your burrowed minions; they can surface and strike now that the board is clear.
  5. Strategically burrow, unburrow and strike while your opponent has difficulty removing anything. Use [[Mad Dash]] to move minions and unburrow in the same turn while drawing a card.
  6. Use removal spells like [[Cave-In]] to get your minions below ground while also killing your opoonents' minions.
  7. Hang in there until you can pop off the enemy avatar with any number of fire spells for the win.


Strategies:


Burrowing:

  1. Using minions with Burrowing, you can stay low while advancing and waiting to strike the opponent.
  2. The burn spells and board wipes in the deck strike units in either a location of your choice (i.e. atop a site and where your minions are not burrowed) or deal board-wide damage to units specifically atop sites.
  3. Use cantrips like [[Mad Dash]] to unburrow and strike an adjacent site in the same turn.
  4. Your burrowed minions escape the wrath of spells like [[Cave In]] and [[Earthquake]].


Burn:

  1. [[Flame Wave]], [[Heat Ray]], and [[Minor Explosion]] all do damage to units from both players.
  2. You break the symmetry by playing 3 specific minions: [[Lava Salamander]], [[Askelon Phoenix]] and [[Infernal Legion]].
  3. [[Infernal Legion]]: Does not die to any of your damage spells, burns anything adjacent for 3 each turn, and doesn't hurt or kill either the Salamander or Phoenix due to their anti-fire buff.
  4. [[Lava Salamander]]; Doesn't take any fire spell damage, and can be an extra spellcaster to line up and pop your opponent when on Death's Door at the end of the game.
  5. [[Askelon Phoenix]]: Gets buffed by your indiscriminate burn spells, then strikes for additional damage because of it. Chain spells to strike your opponent for damage and also buff the bird.


This deck is super fun and has lots of flexibility. It can be fast or hang tough until the late game.


Let me know what you think! I'll post event results eventually.

decks.name: Gen Con 2023 Tournament Winner - Jarrett Messing's Impstorm  (Deathspeaker Air/Fire)
decks.primer:
I find myself in the surprising position to provide insight into the deck that won the Sorcery constructed tournament at Gen Con 2023. You might find this less of a deck tech and more of my thought process going into the event. The decisions that led me to this deck were as much personal as game related. The former, the personal, is inherently so specific as to be rarely addressed in analysis, but it is an equally important element in tournament success. I don't have any astonishing insights into how to build a meta-breaking, tournament-dominating deck. This is more of a lesson in how to stumble forward with what you know.


I prepared with a pair of assumptions:


1) It seemed likely that Air/Earth midrange would be the predominant build. Early successes established this as the preeminent powerhouse, and with limited card supply I suspected this would be one of the easier decks to build for folks who didn't pledge or pledge big. Much of the power is in the ordinary and exceptional slots, and many of the key cards are contained in the preconstructed decks, including one of the best avatars for it (Earth). A Pathfinder based version of this deck seemed on the verge of winning the second season of the TTS league. It's just a damn good, consistent deck that runs a lot of the best cards in the game, capable of big bursts of damage, strong board presence, board manipulation, burst healing, with great removal and maneuver.  


2) I would be playing [[Deathspeaker]]. It seemed close in power to the air/earth deck, if a bit less consistently good, and I had far more reps with it in and out of the TTS league. I did not have time to deviate from my comfort zone and get sufficient practice with anything before the con. The goals of the deck are straightforward. Draw as much as possible through recursion, don't allow heavy hitters to stick around, and maximize damage until you can [[Major Explosion]] or [[Nimbus Jinn]] the opponent to Death's Door. Finishers abound. Pretty simple, right? 


My most difficult choice came down to elements: Air/Earth/Fire, Air/Earth or Air/Fire? Air has the wizards for the card draw, so that was automatic, and Alpha Thunderstorm*. Earth has possibly the best overall suite of spells. Fire offers some of the best options for Deathspeaker in [[Vile Imp]] and [[Death Dealer]], one of the best removal spells in [[Infiltrate]], and best damage in Major Explosion. Take all three perhaps? Well, truthfully, there are more good options with the three elements than fit in a deck, and taking all three elements comes with the cost. Occasionally you will bump into a threshold problem and that can throw a wrench in things, especially if you're running triple threshold cards like [[Divine Healing]] and [[Browse]]. This makes you more dependent on Cores which can be ripped away at inconvenient times. There were three main reasons I decided against Earth. The [[Avatar of Earth]], playing into Earth, is especially devastating. She can grapple across the table with impunity as you're bolstering her with your own sites. I want my opponent to stay on their side of the table. Also, I knew of several off-meta Water decks in attendance, and suspected more. Water hampers many of Earth's best spells. Thirdly, Earth seemed like the slower road to the end game. [[Wraetannis Titan]] requires Sphere offensively, [[Craterize]] is a turn and a tax behind Major Explosion, and healing is prolongation, not acceleration. I felt like I would want the most linear path to Death's Door possible, and to win a race in the mirror match. 


Somewhat ironically, my game 5 finals opponent, Adam (Zalem), consistently one of the best Sorcery players throughout the league and playtests, helped solidify my choice and finalize my deck. After hammering out my idea on Curiosa I decided to see if anyone was running something similar. Lo, Zalem had built an Air/Fire Deathspeaker deck! And it was nearly identical! This gave me a huge confidence boost. His differences were one less Thunderstorm and an additional two [[Chaos Twister]]. I liked my four [[Firebolts]], and I hadn't considered the latter at all in any kind of serious format. But upon checking the Twister FAQ, and with some consideration I saw the incredible upside. You are very likely to remove the target, between the void and sites, and with some luck you have a potential 2-for-1 by slinging it into another minion, or direct damage by hitting the opposing avatar. Funnily enough, when I told this to Zalem, he said it was one of his cuts before the event due to inconsistency! 


Key Cards

[[Thunderstorm]]. *A note on Alpha Thunderstorm. This event used the RAW version of Thunderstorm, the Alpha high T version. It's extremely powerful as it ticks down only when you shoot a bolt, and can linger and move until exhausted. 4 mana, 9 damage. This is amazing, almost immediate pressure. Thunderstorm pairs extremely well with some of the other spells and sites in the deck. Fire's Deserts can clear bolt-absorbers, as can Firebolts, assuring the bolts hit the enemy avatar. I wasn't going to play this event without three. This card will be brought in line for Beta. Three Thunderstorms was a winning choice.


[[Infiltrate]]

Arguably the best removal spell in the game, this card takes your opponent's minion from them and gives you control of that minion with stealth until they deal damage. Notably, when attacking an undefended enemy site, you cause a loss of life rather than damage. Incredible potential, and a huge swing when you can eliminate a beater. I was particularly keen on this as if I stole a 5-power minion from an Earth deck I would now be able to trade their minion with another of their 5-power beaters. 


[[Summoning Sphere]]

Part of the win condition of this deck, a Summoning Sphere + Imp can finish an avatar on Death's Door. It allows me to play a Djinn and dump my hand to bring an avatar to 0. Alternatively, a sphere opener can allow me to play an Imp on their avatar turn 2, which puts a lot of pressure on the opponent to spend removal or get their own minion out at home. 


[[Vile Imp]]

The magnificent Imp! Pinpoint damage, harassment, finishing blow all in an inexpensive and annoying body. 


Apprentice/[[Grandmaster Wizard]]

Draw/Draw more. X2. Maybe x3 or x4 with Geistwood and Pact.


[[Major Explosion]]

The finisher. It's very hard to do sufficient chip damage to finish off an avatar, even with Thunderstorm. Seven mana is not that difficult to cast, and you're often one move away from launching this across the table. The 5 damage splash zone clears Earth heavies. It has the added benefit of clearing the immediate area of Thunderstorm bodyguards. 


[[Highland Falconer]]/[[Sacred Scarabs]]

Exploding flying bugs! Easy four damage and 2-for-1 retrieval. I got rid of scarabs with mulligans every game I drew them in my opening hand. Better to draw some kind of ramp or a recurrable falconer to fetch one. 


So it all worked out! It took some luck as it always does, but the deck performed extremely and consistently well. I stayed within myself, and the flow of play was very familiar despite the lack of reps with this particular build. Most importantly, I played five great opponents who were a pleasure to share the table with, foremost among them being Adam in the final. Nerves came with the stakes, but the game could not have been more friendly. And, despite his rough opening, he had me on Death's Door and was one turn away from snatching away the victory! Wild end to the event!

filteredDecks.name: Tri Speaking Ill of the Dead (4-2 at GenCon)
filteredDecks.primer:
This is my silly little high synergy, value, control deck that I think I'm decent enough to give a primer on at this point. The general idea you are trying to go in with this deck is just survive until you get a tempo advantage. Or even simpler, just survive. This deck is like an ant colony in that all the individual parts are kinda terrible but once you put them all together it's extremely hard to stop.


Generally you going to want to mulligan aggressively for (1), (2), and (3) cost cards that draw, give mana or remove enemy cards with exceptions against specific decks. Against [[Enchantress]] always keep [[Ajaro Exorcist]], against [[Battlemage]] and other voltron style decks keep [[Toolbox]] for [[Dispel]], against [[Savior]] keep [[Bane of Aventis]] and against [[Imposter]] keep [[Legion of Gall]].

For sites, mulligan to get as many different kinds of threshold possible generally. Although it sometimes is wise to keep single threshold sites if it works for curving out your hand. If you have a [[Toolbox]] maybe keep that [[Dark Tower]] for early plays. Some matchups benefit greatly from site as well, [[Wormelow Tump]] being the best thing to keep against opponents that may have cemetery hate. [[Fields of Camlann]] is also great for aggro matchups. Notably if you get [[Orpheus' Crossing]] in your opening hand, only keep it if you think your opponent 1. won't have burn early on and 2. you have something that can put stuff in the cemetery early on i.e [[Cemetery Rats]], [[Shallow Grave]] or [[Forgotten Tomb]]. Its best to think of [[Orpheus' Crossing]] as a spell rather than a land, don't always play it if there is any possibility you could die.


Early turns should be spent playing early value drops that fill up your cemetery or give card advantage like [[Cemetery Rats]], [[Land Surveyor]] and [[Sisters of Avalon]]. If you hit a dead draw in the matchup [[Sisters of Avalon]] is one of the best cards in the deck for filtering cards, like pitching [[Courtesan Thais]] as its only use to play from the cemetery once you get your opponent to death's door. Also [[Landmass]] on turn 3 into [[Skeleton Mage]] playing the [[Landmass]] again is like my favorite shit ever.


Once your opponent starts playing stuff, kill everything they play. Okay not everything, often times a big skill check with this deck is not figuring out how to kill something, its just should you. Threat evaluation is important. Often times you can get away with building up your board even more and just chump blocking whatever they throw in front of you, and then you get to piss them off by playing those cards again! Also always check to see if you can use your opponents genesis abilities and ordinary magics against them as [[Deathspeaker]] and [[Skeleton Mage]] are not exclusive to your own cemetery. Although remember to always savor your life total, I've found its easy to get lost chump blocking or taking a bit of chip here and there and then you find yourself to far behind to catch up.


After you get back tempo its a pretty simple way of winning, just kill them with a thousand little dudes over many turns and kill all there stuff some more. Also [[The Doom of Dilmun]] just kinda wins games sometimes.


Other miscellaneous synergies that are important for the deck include [[The Doom of Dilmun]] not being banished after playing it from your cemetery, allowing you to trash it early on as it functionally is an extra card in hand. [[Pact with the Devil]] is never cast on yourself, always sacrifice a spellcaster with it. You can also sac [[Merlin's Tower]] if you really need those cards. Often [[Common Sense]] is just there to smooth out you curve, getting a [[Landmass]] or [[Land Surveyor]] for the next turn usually isn't bad. Remember [[The Inquisition]] when your opponent is searching your hand or deck. [[Amulet of Niniane]] is one of the best cards in this deck as you get fetch it with [[Highland Princess]] and it prevents most ways an opponent will trying to kill you at death's door, allowing you to use your powered up ability for longer. Also it's one of the only ways to guarantee [[Orpheus' Crossing]]. [[Skeleton Mage]] is the best card in the deck and no one will talk shit on its name, as I said before it can ramp you even further, fix your draws with [[Common Sense]], and often it just wins me games as it sits in my cemetery with a [[Common Sense]] to find [[Lightning Bolt]]. [[Vivien the Enchantress]] is a special addition as it functions really well with all the spellcasters in the deck. If you discard Vivien you can still play it from the cemetery to copy the genesis effects of all spellcasters in the realm. Also sometimes it just wins the game as long as your opponent doesn't remove it (which can be pretty funny against an [[Ironclad]]), playing two minions from the cemetery a turn is a lot better than one, and remember to draw/play a site with her!


This deck still struggles against decks that can slam down a powerful game ending threat each turn like water necro and is part of the reason I used to have [[Drown]] and [[Boil]] in my collection. Its gotten a little more even with the addition of (F) cards that allow for efficient threat removal but its something I would consider adding if you expect a lot of necro. There are some cards I would considering taking out if you have other options or want to test the waters like [[Morgana le Fay]] as she is very threshold heavy early on, [[Bane of Aventis]] who has rarely ever come up in my games or [[Archangel Michael]] as he is very threshold heavy and at the time of writing is like 90$ what the fuck.


Possible additions include everything in the maybeboard but I would mostly consider [[Funeral Pyre]] and [[Mismanaged Mortuary]] as cemetery hate. [[Amethyst Core]], [[Onyx Core]] and [[Ruby Core]] for better fixing. [[Boil]] as said before. [[Jack the Ripper]] and [[Varistus the Evictor]] for mortal and voidwalk heavy decks respectively. Also [[Clamor of Harpies]], [[Hotwheel]] or [[Sir Morien]] if you want actual (4) drops. Also [[Mountain Peaks]] and [[Fertile Earth]] for other good fixing.
